We introduce a span laser with the help of a digital feedback control loop, using an alkali atom vapor cell as the system. Inside the feedback loop, a cavity modifies the laser light, while a digital processor processes data from a photodetector and adjusts the laser's polarization, all in a closed-loop system. This digital control allows for the stabilization of the span laser's operating point, despite the presence of disturbances, primarily caused by magnetic fields, within the data vapor cell. This digital approach offers significant advantages over analog systems, including the ability to easily modify the control strategy and analyze data. This level of precision is crucial for data vapor cells to serve platforms such as the atomic fountain clocks, magnetometers, and quantum computing systems.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism of positive geometric multiplicity, it's proven that the set of Picard values has no finite accumulation points. This leads to a consequence where Siegel disks cannot appear in K3 surfaces that admit a real analytic automorphism with positive geometric multiplicity.

A comprehensive analysis is conducted on the LHC and indirect search results for a light, sub-GeV range dark matter model featuring a Z2 parity. This z-matter model, which includes a neutralino as the primary z-matter candidate, can decay into an antiproton and an electron, along with a gamma ray spectrum resulting from the process. Results indicate that decays of neutralinos into antiprotons are more restrictive than those into positrons for specific mass ranges of 0.1-1 GeV, yet still allow for a sub-GeV range of neutralino masses and sub-GeV range of neutralino masses as viable z-matter candidates. Furthermore, decaying neutralinos produce gamma ray spectra detectable by the Fermi-LAT telescope, specifically in energy ranges around 100 MeV and in gamma ray spectra from dark matter annihilation, which are constrained by H.E.S.S. and MAGIC telescopes, resulting in masses of neutralino and dark matter candidates being in the sub-GeV range of masses.

We present a novel, polynomial-time approximation algorithm for estimating the genus of a non-planar graph with an asymptotic performance guarantee of 3/2. Initially, Hartman and Korach spearheaded this field with their 1983 analysis, and subsequent research by Dyer et al. further explored the topic in 2002 by offering an asymptotic performance approximation for the genus within the NP-hard computational framework.

A proposed algorithm combines a stochastic Newton descent approach with an average consensus method to tackle distributed convex optimization problems, even in cases where objective function gradients or Hessians cannot be freely accessed. This method allows each agent to individually estimate the necessary gradient and Hessian information, but exploits the rapid convergence of a stochastic Newton method, which demands accurate Hessian information.

This study examines how transfer learning affects the detection of hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali using an LSTM model. Transfer learning is employed to mitigate the issue of data scarcity in low-resource languages. To that end, a model is trained on English data and then fine-tuned on Hindi and Bengali datasets. An exploration of hyperparameter settings and the effect of pre-trained word embeddings on the performance of the model in the two low-resource languages is also presented. The findings indicate hyperparameter effects are minimal in these languages, but the choice of word embedding significantly affects the model's performance.

Next-generation dark matter experiments utilizing gas-based time projection chambers rely heavily on recoil event identification. This review examines recent advancements in these observables, which include real-time data tracking, signal voltage analysis, and topological signal assessment. These techniques are extensively used in research on dark matter, neutrino interactions, nuclear physics, and astrophysics.

Assessments of commercial driving skills are increasingly being automated, utilizing computer-aided assessment systems to identify trainees who are unsafe to operate vehicles. Although these systems have shown success in identifying unsafe drivers, they often struggle to recognize the contextual nuances of driving behavior, such as the effectiveness of driver responses in specific situations. This paper proposes a novel approach to mitigating this limitation by integrating machine learning and human expertise in a data-driven process. Our method involves a data collection process that identifies critical moments in assessments where human feedback is essential, and developing a machine-learning interface to efficiently gather this feedback. This interface enables experts to review and provide feedback on individual cases, as well as aggregate results to identify patterns and discrepancies between automated and human assessments. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a case study using data from a driving assessment program for commercial vehicles operating on buses and trucks.

This report presents a detailed explanation of our method for addressing the
out-of-category challenge in the proposed challenge. We are currently working on
a solution to the in-域 segmentation challenge and our current approach involves
discovering a common shape within objects using sparse supervision. We will be
discussing potential future research directions at the end of this report.

This study reveals that in certain growth-roughness exponent scenarios, geodesic paths within Gaussian random field manifolds exhibit statistical independence, allowing for the development of an efficient algorithm to identify these paths. Furthermore, the paper leverages its findings to investigate properties of random walks and other motion types in these field manifolds. Geodesics are explored using both numerical simulations and analytical methods, with simulations confirming that a mass function with a power law index of $-3$ serves as a universal distribution for local masses on geodesic paths, regardless of manifold parameters. Analytical reasoning supports this conclusion by connecting geodesic behavior to critical percolation geodesic properties. The study also finds that two points connected by a geodesic are linked by a significantly shorter shortest path, with this shortcut length scaling as the square root of the distance between the points.
We provide a length-based interpretation of the complex Zeta function via a length-based formula derived from periodic patterns over a finite alphabet.

For cusp forms $f$ of level 1, the distribution of sizes of Fourier coefficients of the L-functions remains uniform. We define the distinctive values of $L(f,\frac{1}{2},\mathbb{1})$ along with their relation to the full L-functions at the critical point. Furthermore, we examine the distribution of sizes of the product of distinct prime-specific L-functions, $\prod_{i=1}^m L(f_i,\frac{1}{2})$, and establish an upper limit for the maximum size of Fourier coefficients of cusp forms to ensure the boundedness of the denominators of these distinctive values.

In a study of armchair graphene nanoribbons with a magnetic core, the application of an external electric field is found to significantly impact spin-dependent charge transport. By analyzing this system with the Dirac equation, the researchers discovered that for narrow graphene widths, a conductance quantization pattern emerges that is sensitive to spin, field intensity, and width. However, for wider graphene widths, this pattern becomes intricate, and is influenced by the interplay between transverse energy levels and the magnetic core's density of states. The researchers also found the existence of a critical point at which quantized conductance transitions from up to down, and this critical point is determined by the interplay between the electric field intensity and the width of the armchair structure. Furthermore, the researchers discovered the existence of a Carchese effect within this system, characterized by resonant scattering of massless Dirac fermions, which gives rise to unusual interference effects, such as a Fano-like effect, in the charge current. The existence of this effect was confirmed by the researchers through their analysis of the system's charge current.

Recent studies have explored the notion of weakly nonlinear and monotone operators within the framework of Riesz spaces. Operators exhibiting this characteristic can be seen as the most basic form of monotone and nonnegative-multiplicative operators that conform to the axioms of abstract measure theory. This paper presents approximation theorems for sequences of such operators targeting a linear operator acting on the space of bounded real functions over a compact Hausdorff space, employing a Korovkin-theorem like approach. The theorems rely on the approximation of three fundamental functions: the constant, the identity, and the square functions. Additionally, the discussion extends to the properties of operators approximating the absolute value, with an examination of its positivity, corollaries involving trigonometric polynomials, and the connection to the Weierstrass approximation theorem.

The study of pancyclicity in graphs involves determining the largest set of vertices with the smallest degree, denoted $k$, such that the graph contains a pancyclic Hamiltonian cycle. Researchers have proposed a conjecture stating that a connected, non-$K_{k,k}$ bipartite graph with a minimum degree of $k$ and a large number of vertices will contain cycles of all possible lengths. This study validates the conjecture and demonstrates that such a graph is also Hamiltonian and contains cycles of all possible lengths. Furthermore, similar results are presented for non-$(k,k)$ $A$-regular graphs, as well as $k$-partite graphs, as well as $k$-partite graphs.

The $v_3$ transverse momentum analog asymmetry ($v_{\perp}$) of transverse momentum spectra of hadrons is analyzed in Pb+Pb, Ru+Ru, and Au+Au collisions using the ALICE detector at a specific energy. This parameter, equivalent to the difference in directed flow between left- and right-transverse momentum collisions, is sensitive to the initial conditions of the collisions. By comparing results from collisions with the same energy in different isobaric and Au+Au systems, the influence of the initial state on the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma can be isolated. This parameter is measured for hadronic systems spanning a specific mass range up to a certain transverse momentum. It is observed that in Pb+Pb and Ru+Ru collisions, $v_{\perp}$ decreases with transverse momentum, a phenomenon consistent with a hydrodynamic model incorporating a varying threshold temperature for partonic fluid. Furthermore, this observation aligns with similar measurements in Au+Au collisions, providing insight into the similar properties of the quark-gluon plasma in different systems at a specific energy.

To effectively model nonlinear systems with infinite states and dynamics, data-driven methods like the Spectral Koopman approach have shown remarkable results. However, issues such as the curse of dimensionality and the overfitting problem in high-dimensional koopman models hinder their practicality. We propose novel assumptions and a corresponding algorithm to mitigate these limitations, especially for systems with sparse dynamics and limited datasets, in dimensions where the curse of dimensionality would typically prevail. We demonstrate through a case study the effectiveness of our method in modeling Earth's atmospheric jet stream using a Lattice Boltzmann model, achieving accurate results even in the presence of noise.

A method for simulating strong field ionization in atoms and molecules has been developed. It involves combining the adiabatic orbital approach with a complex scaling method. By integrating these methods, we can calculate the ionization energy of electrons deeply bound in atoms. To further validate this method, we compared our results with both experimental data and a more comprehensive MCTDHF approach for molecules. Additionally, we demonstrated the scaling energy dependence of the ionization process. This new approach has the advantage of being both computationally efficient and accurate. It has the potential to provide valuable insights into the strong field ionization process in molecules.

The convergence of the Sinkhorn algorithm is studied in a matrix or kernel context where at least one marginal is fixed to ensure algorithm stability, and where the target distribution does not satisfy the Schrödinger problem. Under these conditions, it is demonstrated that the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the target distribution and the distribution obtained from the Sinkhorn algorithm diverges as it converges to the correct solution. Furthermore, when the target distribution satisfies a Pinsker type assumption, the rate of convergence is established along with its limit. This result is verified through numerical experiments involving the Gaussian kernel and also applies to entropic regularized projection for semi-discrete optimal transport.

Measurements of the production cross-section for $t\bar{t}$ have been carried out using proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, with 23.3 inverse femtobarns of collected data. These measurements were performed across three distinct $t\bar{t}$ event categories: two single-topical, three-tuple, and four-tuple states. These findings align with the predictions made by the next-to-leading-order QCD standard model.

A key feature of a strongly interconnected quantum system, where individual components interact with the same reservoir, is its localization behavior. In this context, the quantum system's eigenstates can be divided into two categories: those where the central component interacts with the reservoir, forming the collective subspace, and those where the central component is decoupled, forming the embedded subspace. It is during the latter's dynamics that localization occurs. We investigate the localization behavior in such systems, specifically when the spectrum of the reservoir is either continuous or exhibits a finite discontinuity. We establish that when the spectrum is continuous, the conditional probability distribution of the quantum system exhibits a power law decay, whereas it shows exponential decay in the case of a finite discontinuity. We validate these findings through numerical simulations of a quantum spin chain and the non-Hermitian quantum Ising Hamiltonian.

This article aims to explore connections between generalized Bessel functions and specific subclasses of analytic univalent functions, particularly those tied to the Janowski class. To this end, we will derive bounds on derivative orders and provide exact values in certain scenarios. Our analysis will rely on a function, $B_n(z)$, which has specific properties such as $B_n(0)=0$ and $|B_n^{(k)}(0)| \leq (1-|b|^k)/k!$ for specific values of $k$ and $b$. We will utilize these properties to obtain our results within the class $I_n$ consisting of univalent functions with specific coefficient constraints.

The COVID-19 pandemic's impact on urban life has been profound, yet insights into its effects on urban diversity remain scarce due to limitations in existing data sets. By leveraging the Hyperion city-branding platform, which tracks urban destinations, our research demonstrates how pandemic-related changes in human mobility patterns led to significant alterations in the geographic and demographic diversity of urban encounters. During the pandemic, the distribution of business locations in the Hyperion network became more heterogeneous, contrasting with the more homogenized spatial pattern of human movement. Furthermore, the digital interactions among urban residents exhibited greater heterogeneity compared to their geographic digital connections during the pandemic. Notably, the pandemic's influence varied across different city sectors, with the financial and professional industries experiencing increased income homogeneity in their digital interactions, whereas other industries experienced the opposite trend.

This study investigates how fluid facilitation functions are influenced by local saturation, thereby adapting to the specific characteristics of the surrounding medium. Building upon previous models, such as the classical cos $\theta_s$ saturation-dependent facilitation and its direct counterpart, we propose an additional variant, dubbed 'dual facilitation', and assess its performance. Employing numerical simulations, we explore two-phase flow within heterogeneous porous media and find that the 'dual facilitation' model outperforms others, significantly reducing large-scale variance in velocity fields and improving fluid channeling through high permeability areas. Notably, the introduction of the 'dual facilitation' model also results in more realistic residual oil saturation values.

The inherent chirality of optical materials causes light to behave asymmetrically in relation to the direction it travels. This phenomenon is known as directional chirality. For multi-dimensional photonic structures, it was hypothesized that they could exhibit both spatial and temporal symmetry breaking. However, a chirality of optical structures that responds differently to left and right circularly polarized light was not considered possible. This concept is referred to as single-handedness. In this paper, a class of single-handed optical structures was discovered and their properties analyzed. These structures can be used to create complex photonic devices. For example, a proposed 1D grating can act as a filter for both wavelength and polarization. Additionally, it can be used to store information in a unique way. Furthermore, it can be used to create directional devices that can distinguish between the polarity of light.

Our analysis of JT gravity through the path integral formulation reveals the theoretical framework's direct correlation to two distinct quantum mechanical systems: a singular matrix model and a theory of Liouville conformal field. The study examines how these systems reduce to the JT gravity action, with particular attention to the Boltzmann factor in the matrix model and the insertion of the Liouville vertex operator with conformal dimension $(c,0)$. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between JT gravity and SYK, with JT's geometric characteristics and boundary condition requirements leading to the emergence of a massive vertex operator. The discussion also highlights the emergence of an additional boundary in the presence of a dilaton extremum and how this is represented in the corresponding quantum systems.

Recent research on warp drive solutions has led to the discovery of two distinct solutions with a non-zero expansion rate, one of which has been identified as potentially realizable with a finite amount of energy. An examination of the energy requirements for these solutions has revealed the possibility of converting their initially required negative energy into a positive value by modifying the shape of the funnel. In the current study, we expand on these findings by exploring the potential of a new class of warp drive solutions that incorporate a positive cosmological constant. We derive a set of differential equations that determine the required properties of the ideal fluid, expressing them as functions of the shape factor, radius, and expansion rate. Furthermore, we establish relationships between the pressure and density of the fluid using the general relativistic equation of state. Our findings demonstrate the existence of specific radius and expansion rate values, or alternatively, pressure and density combinations, for which the energy negativity issue can be eliminated.

Urban areas are increasingly adopting a digital approach to manage and monitor physical infrastructure, such as streetlights and buildings, by locating and tracking these elements within their vicinity.  To facilitate this, many cities are now employing digital duplicates of their urban environments, often based on open-source software.  Despite its potential, successful implementation is hindered by significant challenges, primarily the lack of detailed information about the physical installation of their urban infrastructure, such as the height of their streetlights or nearby objects, within existing geospatial datasets.  To address this issue, we introduce GUIDES - an innovative platform that streamlines the process of collecting and managing this information by allowing users to easily edit and append data to existing installation records or create new ones with minimal effort.

We conduct an in-depth analysis of spin-coherent destruction of oscillations (CDW) in both single and multi-component linear ion crystals. This technique is highly sensitive to motional energy, making it an effective tool for measuring mode temperatures, state distributions, and heating rates. By utilizing CDW to investigate the temperature and distribution of motional states in a two-component yttbium yttbium crystal, and comparing it with measurements from quantum-jump-based sideband thermometry, we derive a model of the CDW phenomenon. This model, informed by Monte Carlo simulations of Paul trap heating, is then used to interpret our experimental findings.

This study assesses the role of various parameters in TERS, including the dimensions of the tip and substrate, laser polarization, and the dimensions of the plasmonic aperture, by applying a quantum mechanical model. The interaction between light and matter is simulated using Mie theory and Fermi's golden rule. A silver hemispherical tip model is employed, and the results show that the electromagnetic field is concentrated around the tip's apex. The position of the laser polarization relative to the substrate is crucial in the electromagnetic enhancement, and the electromagnetic field is localized at the substrate's edge. The electrochemical enhancement is evaluated by considering a single molecule with an electron affinity of 2.66 eV and the tip as a semiconductor material. The model predicts a localized electric field of approximately 10^10 V/m and a current density of 10^10 A/m^2 near the tip's apex. The results also show that chemical and electromagnetic mechanisms can be combined to improve TERS resolution.

Galaxies in the Local Volume were observed using the 64-meter Sardinia Radio Telescope at a frequency of 3.1 GHz. By analyzing emission in the K-band, we aimed to identify any anomalous microwave signals. The observations, which covered 24 galaxies within a redshift of z=0.03, showed emission levels between -16 and +16 sigma for the K-band and -10 and +18 sigma for the total K+A band. No significant detection was made, but we could constrain star formation rates, hot gas temperatures, and electron energies. The results suggest that the K+A band emission rate is less than 0.02 times the far-infrared flux density for the sample. The SRT's capabilities, combined with its high angular resolution, make it a powerful tool for observing the K-band, particularly for detecting extragalactic sources with high spatial resolution.

A notable property in certain compounds is their structural entropy-driven relaxation,
characterized by an extensive entropy change and entropy residual. Ammonium sulfate
exhibits structural entropy-driven relaxation, and also displays ferroelectricity.
We investigate the entropy source in ammonium sulfate and perform a comprehensive
entropy decomposition analysis. The results indicate that an extensive entropy change
is primarily caused by the rotational isomers of ammonium ions, whereas the entropy
residual is attributed to the orientationally disordered DS4 cations. Additionally,
the interactions between cations and the sulfate anion are analyzed using
ab-initio calculations. The calculated entropic properties of ammonium sulfate
align with experimental measurements.

To thrive in life, creatures must adapt their behavior based on their experiences. A widely accepted theory suggests that organisms learn through unexpected events, and this mechanism drives the acquisition of valuable habits. However, it's been argued that the brain's response to unexpected events is merely a byproduct of a more fundamental system. We investigated this idea in a controlled experiment, and our results show that an advanced brain region, called the ventral tegmental area, encodes prediction errors in real-time. We discovered that individuals who exhibited a stronger response in this brain region tended to explore new options more effectively, especially in complex scenarios with many choices. Furthermore, our findings suggest that effective strategies for discovering new information are inherent in the way the brain processes errors in prediction, and these strategies vary across individuals.

A quantum system's behavior is described by a core system, which has a core rank equal to its dimension. The core system's elements are corecipients, which are core systems with a rank equal to one. Core systems are interconnected through a core space, which is defined by a core relation that describes the orthogonality between core systems and corereciprocals. In the case of a quantum system, the core systems are q-systems, which are core systems with a core rank equal to their dimension. The core systems are interconnected through a core space, which is defined by a core relation that describes the orthogonality between core systems and corereciprocals. In the case of a q-system, the core systems are q-systems, which are core systems with a core rank equal to their dimension. The core systems are interconnected through a core space, which is defined by a core relation that describes the orthogonality between core systems and corereciprocals. In the case of a q-system, the core systems are q-systems, which are core systems with a core rank equal to their dimension.

The approximate close-neighbor (ACN) problem for time series, a crucial computational issue, has been a significant challenge. The primary challenge involves identifying all pairs of curves within a curve database that are approximately close under a distance metric. While the ACN problem has a significant impact on various applications, the existing algorithms have significant drawbacks, primarily involving high query times and large update costs. Specifically, the existing algorithms rely on the triangle inequality, but this often leads to substantial query times. In this research, we address the ACN problem for time series under the Frechet distance, and we establish rigorous theoretical bounds for both the update and query times. The proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance, and we demonstrate its efficacy through empirical evaluations. The study also explores additional properties and provides insights into the effectiveness of the approach.

A crucial method in quantum computing is mitigating computational errors. Our solution addresses the challenge of iteratively applying corrections in cases where outcomes are interconnected. Using a iterative Bayesian approach known as "unfolding," we can process any circuit layout with any level of noise. Our approach has two key advantages: it's straightforward to implement for complex circuits and can be executed efficiently using current technology. Our experimental findings show that iterative corrections can substantially enhance quantum computing's accuracy in the current "NISQ" era. Our method also holds promise in the future "quantum advantage" era.

Currently, robot standards are separate from one another, with the exception of physical standards that share a common frame of reference, typically grounded in gravity. This paper introduces a new concept of shared autonomy, an objective other than gravity, enabling robot standards to intersect. Implementing shared autonomy requires agents to anticipate outcomes following actions they both perceive as necessary for completion. By applying this idea to robot standards, agents can recognize standards that intersect, thereby facilitating mutual learning and validation of their standards, ultimately leading to shared autonomy itself. Shared autonomy, in turn, enables the emergence of cooperative behavior, thereby solving the problem of implicit coordination. By leveraging shared autonomy, a multi-agent system can be built to demonstrate its utility, thereby facilitating the learning and execution of complex tasks such as driving a vehicle, piloting a drone, and controlling a robotic arm.

Effective navigation in unfamiliar environments relies heavily on reliable map representations. Existing representations excel in building and interpreting known maps, but fall short in addressing real-world challenges such as rapid construction and by-design unpredictability. To address these issues, we propose HiTMap, a novel map representation based on topological diagrams that excels in both quickly constructing and interpreting maps of unfamiliar environments. By organizing information hierarchically, HiTMap streamlines the navigation process and minimizes the likelihood of getting lost. The compact nature of HiTMap allows robots to explore efficiently and locate the optimal path to their goal, even with limited resources. Using a hierarchical A* algorithm, our proposed navigation method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques by significantly reducing computation time and offering a valuable framework for navigating unfamiliar terrains.

Two-dimensional zero-cross-correlation array codes can offer superior performance over one-dimensional zero-correlation codes. However, determining the number of such codes and their optimal size remains an unresolved issue. We have developed a novel method for constructing two-dimensional supplementary array codes using multivariable functions, achieving a higher count and optimal spacing of correlation peaks. Our results show that these codes can attain high two-dimensional correlation performance with a group count on par with current best practices.

We address the challenge of recovering the source function from noisy and incomplete measurements in the context of a multi-energy Computed Tomography (CT) system. Our approach formulates a reconstruction problem as a multi-component inverse task, leveraging the unique characteristics of incoherent and coherent spectral data. Each material's absorption coefficient is reconstructed from the incoherent spectrum, while the source function is determined using both coherent and back-calculated spectrum measurements. A non-convex variational model is introduced to reconstruct the source function and incoherent spectrum, complemented by a convolution-based filter for removing sensor noise from the incoherent spectrum. Our model enables the simultaneous reconstruction of the source function, back-calculated spectrum, and material transmittors, effectively leveraging all system data to improve the quality of the reconstructions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the model's effectiveness in high-quality reconstructions of the source function and material transmittors, even with low-dose data, and its capability to significantly enhance the quality of the reconstructions by utilizing the shared source function and material transmittors across multiple energy levels.

This research investigates how surface states in a metal-dielectric interface change as the dielectric layer's thickness is reduced. The study compares local density of states calculations based on the rigid wall and jellium models to see how well each models predict the surface state behavior. The results indicate that in the jellium model, the surface state is suppressed when the dielectric layer's thickness is comparable to or less than the metal's electron density spill-out length. The study also found that in the jellium model, the surface state is suppressed earlier than in the rigid wall model, indicating a significant impact of nonlocal effects. However, in a bilayer structure, both the jellium model and the rigid wall model predict similar surface state behaviors when the dielectric layer's thickness is comparable to the electron spill-out length. The study demonstrates that accurate modeling of surface states in thin films requires consideration of the electron spill-out and nonlocal effects, particularly when the dielectric layer's thickness is within a few nanometers.

In contextual named entity retrieval, determining which terms in a question aid in identifying the appropriate entities is crucial. This is because questions often contain ambiguous entity candidates, eliminating irrelevant ones reaps a significant advantage. A well-established assessment method for evaluating the relative importance of terms is information gain. However, calculating information gain for each term within a question, given a corpus of questions and answers, is computationally costly. A more efficient approach involves utilizing the term's position in the question, analogous to utilizing question words in Chinese, to gauge its relevance. This involves assigning scores to individual terms based on their relevance to the answer entity, given a question word, and then aggregating these scores to determine the overall gain for each term in the question. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in contextual named entity retrieval.

Time series and longitudinal data, which change over time, are often visualized using time-series charts, but their complexity can be overwhelming due to multiple simultaneous trends. The addition of contextual data, such as text or numbers, further complicates matters. In this study, we investigate how users interact with and explore complex scenarios, which involve multiple time-series data points, accompanied by contextual data. Our research reveals that users struggle to grasp the temporal progression of the data, especially when contextual information is present. To address this, we propose that future tools should incorporate mechanisms to facilitate users' ability to make informed decisions and take actions based on their understanding of the data's temporal evolution.

Recent advancements in various fields have been driven by the success of deep learning, a field that is also being applied to medical data analysis with promising results. However, deep learning's ability to generalize to new environments and its requirement for large amounts of data pose significant limitations. A more effective alternative could be a graph neural network (GNN), which is a more data-efficient and generalizable form of deep learning, specifically designed for graph data. A key challenge lies in learning a meaningful graph structure from unstructured data, a problem that is particularly challenging when dealing with large-scale, complex records such as those found in the medical field. A proposed solution to this issue is a new gain-resemblance graph neural network (HR-GNN) model, which creates a resemblance graph based on the heterogeneity of medical data, using a unique graph construction method. This model has been successfully applied to medical data using electronic health records and has shown promising results in a disease classification task, with the code for the model available on the GitHub repository http://github.com/leehyoseok/HR-GNN.

This study explores the impact of solvent polarization on the electric double layer (EDL) of soft surfaces in electrolyte solutions using the Poisson-Boltzmann equation and a lattice Boltzmann method to simulate the fluid dynamics. An analytical approach is employed to model the surface polymer layer, while a numerical method is used to solve the fluid equations and calculate current density and polarization density. The results indicate that the inclusion of solvent polarization leads to the formation of a distinct polymer layer and affects the distribution of ions near the surface. Additionally, it is found that the presence of free ions can counteract the effect of solvent polarization on the polymer layer, while Ions of opposite charge to the surface charge are attracted to the surface and ions of the same charge are repelled.

Our approach utilizes state machine extraction to automatically identify software specifications from text-based resources like user manuals and design documents. These extracted models facilitate a deeper understanding of the software's functional requirements, making them useful for generating unit tests, ensuring that the software's text-based description aligns with its code implementation. Our study utilized unstructured and structured documents to test the effectiveness of our method, and we applied the Z3 solver to verify the consistency of the extracted models, finding that the method successfully identified text-based specifications with some accompanying errors, which we discuss along with the method's practical applications.

A key challenge in energy-constrained wireless networks is optimizing energy efficiency, a metric that balances energy consumption and network performance. To address this issue, a novel technique has been proposed to balance energy usage in a wireless network, incorporating a cooperative network coding scheme that involves multiple relays in series. The goal is to minimize energy usage at each network node by determining optimal energy allocations for information transmission and reflected data. To achieve this goal, algorithms have been developed to successively determine optimal energy allocations for both source and relay nodes. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed technique, resulting in significant energy savings compared to conventional energy allocations.

A first-principles model combining spin-orbit coupling and electron-phonon interactions is used to study the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in a system involving an Mn adatom and Mn clusters on Nb(110). The impact of structural and magnetic disorder on the RDH and spin polarization in the gap is examined. The effects of varying the magnetic moment of Mn and its surrounding superconducting host are also investigated.

This paper addresses the challenge of eliminating the directional bias in distribution-based 3D pose estimation. The existing approaches rely on either a domain-specific 6-vector distribution or a graph convolution network to represent the pose, but both have their limitations. The former is inherently biased, while the latter is computationally expensive and complex to implement. To address these issues, a simple, effective, and efficient 2-vector distribution is proposed, consisting of 3D translation and 2D planar rotation angles. The framework's parameters are designed to achieve rotational invariance and representation equivariance, ensuring that the framework is rotationally invariant. The framework's rotational invariance is further enhanced by a rotationally invariant feature descriptor, leading to a rotationally invariant 3D pose estimator. The proposed approach is validated on the ApolloScape dataset and demonstrates superior performance compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods.

Generating synthetic training data for deep networks requires significant computational resources and time due to the labor-intensive process of creating labeled data. This process often involves substantial human intervention, which can be costly and time-consuming. To mitigate these challenges, we developed an efficient method for producing training datasets, utilizing a fast and effective image edge detection algorithm. Our approach leverages convolution and Laplacian filtering techniques to achieve a detection rate of over 90% relative to manually annotated data. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of this method by applying it to analyze satellite imagery in search of geological formations, which may indicate areas of potential mineral deposits. Our innovative solution enables the creation of high-quality training data without relying on deep networks, thereby optimizing the entire dataset production process.

High-energy, intense X-ray pulses can cause damage to the fine details of an element's electronic structure spectrum at the edge of its absorption energy range. This damage is due to the ionization of inner-shell electrons and the subsequent displacement of other electrons. This process is known as the Auger effect and can be difficult to study due to the complexity of the involved electron interactions. In this study, we have developed a new model that takes into account the non-linear interactions of electrons and the impact of density ionization on the absorption spectrum. Our model is based on the movement of electrons and provides a mathematical description of how an element's electronic structure changes over time. By applying this model to the absorption spectrum of a specific element, we have shown that a two-stage process is responsible for a significant increase in absorption, with the Auger effect playing a crucial role. Our model has been validated using experimental data and has demonstrated that a specific element's absorption spectrum can be described accurately by considering the linear and non-linear ionization processes.

Research into the reliability of Machine Learning (ML) models has been significantly impacted by the introduction of adversarial attacks, which exploit vulnerabilities in data classification. A proposed method to counter these attacks involves the creation of a conditional generative adversarial network (CGGAN) that can learn to generate adversarial data without requiring access to that data during the process. This CGGAN is used in conjunction with a classifier to maintain a consistent classification rate, thereby improving the reliability of the ML model. This approach is applied to a real-world scenario involving the classification of modulated signals, demonstrating that it can significantly improve the modulated signal classifier's resilience against adversarial attacks, while requiring only the primary training data and a smaller dataset for the CGGAN.

Continuing to learn from where the model last left off can be more effective than training from scratch, especially when dealing with data that has been de-identified, as our experiments demonstrate. We've successfully applied this approach to segment Multiple Sclerosis lesions in MRI scans from different hospital databases, utilizing the U-Net architecture, and compared its performance when retraining versus continuing to learn from where the model last left off, even after a significant time interval. Moreover, our study also highlights the importance of choosing the right loss function, as our results show that the weighted sum loss can outperform the loss used in the original model when retraining the network.

A novel technique for achieving high-precision contrast enhancement in quantum computing, known as Bipolar Contrast, is introduced and has a relatively straightforward implementation. It employs a pair of pi/2 pulses, one with a positive frequency and the other with a negative frequency, applied to the quantum system. This method is particularly effective and is suitable for various types of entangling pulses, including those used in spin and dipole-based quantum systems, and even asymmetric entangling pulses. It is hypothesized that the Bipolar Contrast method is immune to noise affecting the quantum system, including amplitude, frequency, and fluctuations related to laser intensity, frequency, and the Zeeman effect. Furthermore, theoretical simulations have been conducted to demonstrate its efficacy. It is also proposed that this method can be used to experimentally assess the quality of entanglement in quantum systems.

In the realm of data-driven system analysis, machine learning models have been successfully applied to infer system dynamics from data. However, understanding how these models fail is crucial for identifying areas of uncertainty and developing more accurate predictions. This study presents a systematic approach to understanding the failure modes of machine learning models when applied to dynamic systems. We draw upon fundamental system theory to create a set of natural indicators that measure how far a system deviates from equilibrium. We then introduce neural networks to learn these indicators from data, and through this process, we create a visual representation of where and why the learning models fail. This method is demonstrated using a simple pendulum system and a more complex brain imaging dataset, showcasing its effectiveness in pinpointing failure patterns and offering insights into the modeling process.

A distant dust cloud in the direction of Ophiuchus is emitting a strong radio jet, 
indicating the presence of a core where a massive star is in the process of formation.
Researchers have made significant progress in understanding the evolution of this star by
analyzing radio emissions at various frequencies and creating models of the star's core.
The results of this analysis reveal a crucial shift in the star's core from being core-contracted
to core-expanded within a short period of time.
This transformation is likely caused by the star accreting material at a high rate, 
indicating a high mass-accretion rate phase in the process of star formation.
The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the process of massive star formation, 
which is still not fully understood, and highlight the need for further research to 
gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon.

This paper introduces PopSyCLE, a Python framework for the post-formation evolution of Primordial Black Holes, and presents results from simulations. These simulations explore the formation of PBHs from gravitational collapse during a matter-dominated phase, with PBH masses ranging from $10^{15}$ to $10^{24}$ grams. Initial conditions, such as PBH mass and mass fraction, are randomly assigned, and the PBHs are subject to interactions with dark matter and baryonic matter, as well as accretion, mass increase, and object formation, including stars, supermassive black holes, and intermediate-mass black holes. The PopSyCLE model incorporates these processes, where PBH dark matter density evolves over time, and is validated using PBH formation data from other studies.

Building upon a previous study of modulated phases in hard wedge systems, where the fundamental building block was a dimer made of spheres of two distinct sizes, we now extend the investigation to trimers consisting of spheres of varying sizes. Leveraging density functional theory and a fundamental measure theory that accounts for polyomeric shapes, our research identifies and analyzes coexistence conditions and packing fractions within the non-accumulation regime. Notably, we find that the equilibrium boundary between liquid and crystal phases is insensitive to the specific geometry of the trimer, a characteristic also exhibited in the previously observed splay modulated equilibrium boundary and the newly discovered liquid-rich phase boundary within the non-accumulation regime. Through our simulations, we validate these findings and map out the trimer's phase diagram, where phase transitions are dictated by the relative sizes of the constituent spheres and the number and arrangement of the monomers.

Recent advancements in Adjusting Transformer models have gained significant attention, 
particularly the STA method which utilizes a trainable special token to adapt to various 
downstream tasks. Although STA proves effective, we find that for many tasks a substantial 
portion of the model remains largely unmodified, leading to the underutilization of relevant 
information. In an effort to maximize the utilization of this information, we propose a 
novel approach that involves distributing the adaptation process across the model by leveraging 
gradient-based learning to activate previously dormant parameters, thereby increasing their 
contribution to the adaptation process and improving overall task performance. The 
experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding substantial 
gains in multiple benchmark datasets.

To effectively handle the escalating complexity of software configuration management, a systematic approach is required. Introducing preference ordering into this process allows users to express their preferences over specific properties using preferred dispreferences. A partial order is then established among configurable products based on their preference profiles, which determines the best product to recommend to users. Traditionally, partial orders are built by comparing the profiles of products item by item. However, a novel approach considers the whole profile at once. We compare these two methodologies and investigate their respective advantages and limitations.

Recent scientific research has demonstrated that certain properties of polymer liquids are governed by a ratio, combining temperature-dependent characteristics and glass transition temperatures, when the level of supercooling is high. This study further explores this relationship by examining whether a general pattern emerges when the glass transition temperature is replaced with various other characteristic temperatures, including those defined by specific viscosities, molecular relaxation, and relaxation times. Additionally, it examines whether a correlation exists between these characteristic temperatures and the glass transition temperature for a specific polymer, polystyrene, with a broad range of viscosities and relaxation times. Our results show that a specific relationship, or scaling, is maintained, and that the correlation between characteristic temperatures and the glass transition temperature is also effective for a range of viscosities and relaxation times.

Recent studies have revealed that certain aspects of human development, particularly the cognitive processing of social interactions, can be mirrored in artificial intelligence models like large language ones. Building upon this connection, our research delves into applying similar insights to AI models by focusing on a previously unexplored area - the rejection processing developmentally relevant task (JD-TRP). This concept involves a two-stage process where a sample is initially filtered out and then fine-tuned using corrected examples to enhance model accuracy. We applied this method to improve the accuracy of Transformer-based language models on three distinct types of graph reading comprehension tests, which assess the understanding of complex graphical representations. Our results demonstrate that JD-TRP yields better performance than traditional pre-training methods and that the filtering stage, which removes incorrect examples, plays a crucial role in optimizing the model's performance. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the importance of selecting the right level of correction and correctness thresholds to achieve optimal outcomes. Ultimately, our study sheds light on the value of considering developmental principles in AI design and opens up new avenues for integrating human cognitive principles into artificial intelligence development.

For machine translation, a network's target vocabulary significantly influences target word ordering, as words are often selected based on their order in the source sentence. Although some networks incorporate attention mechanisms, they typically choose words without considering upcoming target words. In contrast, this paper introduces a generation method that incorporates a look-ahead mechanism, allowing words to be selected by considering their context and future position in the target translation. By utilizing conditional probabilities, this method can determine the optimal order of words in the target translation. Through ablation studies on the 2018 FLI 3.0 dataset, this method achieves substantial improvements over standard approaches, with an BLEU score increase of 1.16. By fine-tuning networks on a larger dataset, this method can yield even greater gains, with an additional 0.96 BLEE score improvement. By integrating this method with look-back mechanisms, an even greater word ordering influence is achieved.

This study calculates the specific weights for Kontsevich graphs linked to connection and curvature tensor graphs within non-degenerate PO_n varieties. It also examines the corresponding graph formulas for torsion and the Derivative of a PO_n curvature tensor, along with a discussion of possible graph-based expressions for the Levi-Civita connection in this context.

This study explores the properties of large-N CFTs perturbed by a specific operator, whose effect varies from generating flow to no impact, based on specific parameters. Our analysis, conducted in the Euclidean path integral framework, reveals how these parameters influence the behavior of the system, particularly in relation to its entanglement entropy and thermal properties. Our results demonstrate that certain regimes of the perturbation can lead to flow away from the original theory, while others result in the theory remaining unchanged. Our analysis is based upon an expansion in a large-N limit and how the operator modifies the theory's correlators. Our findings also suggest that the entanglement entropy of the system is sensitive to the theory's coupling strength and can be used to probe the theory's RG flow. Our work provides new insights into how large-N CFTs behave under perturbation and how their properties can be influenced by specific parameters.

The proof in the supplementary materials for the referenced paper has an error. We identify this mistake and offer the correct proof for Equation 14 in that study. Additionally, our subsequent equations 20 through 24 are based on flawed reasoning. This note clarifies that an Asian option's price cannot be independently calculated from a Markov process's transition matrix and the option's payoff. We also outline the necessary adjustments to the proof in Equation 14 and present an alternative approach for deriving the short Asian option's call price using a Markov chain approximation of geometric Brownian motion, with simulations showing that the authors' proposed approach yields inaccurate results.

Our analysis of X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton across 21 clusters of galaxies indicates that the discrete population of galaxies within these clusters emit a combined X-ray luminosity roughly equivalent to that of the continuous X-ray emission from the intracluster medium. This discovery suggests that the X-ray emission from the intracluster medium originates from a combination of continuous emission from the ICM and the combined X-ray emission from individual galaxies within the cluster. Consequently, the non-collimated gamma-ray emission generated by the interaction of the ICM and cosmic rays could result in a signal in the GeV range that is on the order of 10^-4 for clusters with a typical size. This level of gamma-ray emission could resolve the long-standing discrepancy in explaining the X-ray and gamma-ray properties of the Wide Angle Survey clusters.

The standard model of cosmology employs an almost-scale-invariant power spectrum to predict the cosmic structure's distribution. However, this prediction cannot fully explain certain observations, notably the large-scale cosmic flow and the accumulation of galaxies within filaments. In contrast, the particle-collider-cosmology model suggests post-inflationary signals that could explain these observations through a new mechanism. Our research aims to refine the signal-to-noise ratio by utilizing data from galaxy surveys, potentially uncovering primary features. Furthermore, we outline a theoretical framework for detecting primary signals through quadratic correlations in cosmic galaxies.

Despite their impressive performance, Deep Convolutional Neural Networks remain opaque, making it challenging to understand their decision-making process. Current explanation methods often overlook the behavior of individual neurons and how they contribute to the network's overall function. This study proposes a new approach, LattentConv, which utilizes saliency maps to visualize which image regions and specific semantic features within those regions are activated during the network's forward pass. By integrating these insights, we can create a detailed visual account of the network's behavior, effectively bridging the gap between low-level semantic analysis and high-level class understanding. Furthermore, our proposed method offers new perspectives on understanding feature hierarchies, as revealed through its application to various image classification tasks.

The two-dimensional $d$-wave superconductivity in cuprates is believed to originate from an attractive interaction between electrons that overcomes their natural repulsion. The primary focus of this study is on one-dimensional structures, such as stripes in cuprates, to understand the mechanism of this attractive interaction. By utilizing the Hubbard model combined with a method that incorporates electron-photon interactions, our findings demonstrate that the repulsion between electrons in one-dimensional cuprates can be reversed and become an attractive force that can even surpass the original repulsion when certain conditions are met. Importantly, this attractive interaction has a long range and depends heavily on the phase matching of phonons. The results of this study provide a crucial insight into the source of attractive interaction that gives rise to superconductivity in cuprates.

A novel CAI dataset is introduced, featuring 285 brain regions from the Human Brain Project, with 391 potential causal connections, each representing a likely link between regions. This enriched information set serves as the basis for developing a individualized structure learning method to discover the underlying causal network of brain regions. This approach integrates observations of brain activity with structural constraints derived from biological knowledge, resulting in a unique causal model for each subject. Notably, the proposed method's performance surpasses that of a group-based learning approach, even when the latter utilizes the full CAI dataset. Furthermore, the model's outcomes are validated through theoretical analyses and experimental results.

The existence of unstable and unstable-like skyrmion lattices, which are characterized by a dynamic state with a specific pitch, has been confirmed in the family of chiral magnets. Studies have also identified a helical phase that exhibits a pitch identical to the one observed in the dynamic state, which is attributed to quantum fluctuations. Our research reveals, through the combination of neutron diffraction and first-principles calculations, that the unstable skyrmion phase in the magnet Co9Zn9Mn2, which has a specific magnetic anisotropy, is associated with thermal fluctuations. As the temperature increases, the unstable skyrmion phase transitions into a stable lattice structure. Notably, the magnetization measurements show that the unstable skyrmion phase has a specific critical temperature, which is significantly lower than the Curie temperature, and the magnetization curve shows a specific plateau that is characteristic of the unstable skyrmion phase, which disappears as the temperature increases. Our research provides a theoretical basis for understanding the stability of skyrmion phases, which is crucial for their potential applications in data storage and processing.

High-dimensional data analysis has become a crucial area of research in the last two decades, with a particular focus on time series analysis. A variable selection technique, which identifies and retains the most relevant variables while eliminating unnecessary ones, has emerged as a fundamental approach for working with such data. The variable selection technique has multiple benefits, including reducing the overall complexity, avoiding overfitting, and improving the interpretability of the results. The current study presents a comprehensive overview of the variable selection methodology when applied to high-dimensional dynamic models, including linear regression models, vector autoregressive models, vector balance models, and vector Markov switching models. The discussion is selective in nature and primarily focuses on the lines of thought and future lines of research.

The equilibrium problem is a far-reaching mathematical framework that includes several well-established problems, such as variational inequalities, optimization tasks, and kernel functions, as specific instances. A iterative algorithm with accompanying theoretical analysis and practical applications is presented, leveraging the connection between the given equilibrium function and the contraction mapping. This relationship is further explored through the development of an abstruse operator that facilitates a comprehensive analysis of the method's efficacy.

A recently developed technique called Bayesian Neural Networks has gained attention in the image processing community for its image restoration and concealment techniques. This work focuses on the potential of BNNs in the field of reversible information concealment. We propose a novel, task-specific, Bayesian network designed for the concealment of binary data within images, employing the maximum a posteriori principle. Our model's efficacy is demonstrated through its performance on the standard NOISECHALLENGE dataset, where it shows improved accuracy and better results compared to state-of-the-art, non-reversible, binary BNN-based concealment methods, notably outperforming the ones presented by Alzate et al. and Wang et al. Our approach also offers significant advantages over state-of-the-art, irreversible, reversible, and task-specific, non-Bayesian concealment methods.

A mean-field approach is used to investigate how various factors influence the dynamics of convective dynamos on a global scale. To achieve this, a mean-field model is developed, accounting for three key turbulent effects: the effect on mean-field transport, helicity, and the interaction between these fields, all derived from second-order closure and scale-dependent eddy covariance calculations. Three-dimensional MHD simulations from a cutting-edge convection code inform these turbulent quantities. As expected, analysis of non-differential rotation regimes reveals the necessary presence of turbulent magnetic forces to achieve self-sustaining solutions. In contrast to previous findings, solutions that incorporate a tachocline exhibit characteristics similar to those of the simulations, including an equatorial super-rotation pattern and a sharp transition between radiative and convective zones. Notably, these solutions also reveal the presence of a shear layer above the core rather than at the boundary between the convective and radiative zones.

The galaxy NGC4945, a Seyfert 2, displays signs of a molecular ejecta, which we've imaged using ALMA at 1.3mm wavelengths. Our observations reveal two key features: a bright core and extended molecular line emission. The data indicate the presence of a shock-driven molecular ejecta, with the shock velocity estimated at approximately 100km/s. Our analysis of the 12CO and 13CO spectra suggests the line profiles are consistent with a shock-driven molecular ejecta, with the 12CO emission being self-absorbed. Our findings support the hypothesis that the molecular ejecta in NGC4945 is powered by the galaxy's central engine, which is consistent with the galaxy's Seyfert 2 classification.

A sophisticated numerical algorithm developed by Gustafsson et al. (2019) is designed to solve complex magnetized plasma problems through quasilinear diffusion equations. This advanced algorithm employs a variational method, incorporating a hybrid approach with finite elements in the spatial dimension and a second-order Runge-Kutta scheme in the temporal dimension. Building upon this work, a new numerical algorithm is presented that incorporates a conservative finite volume scheme in the spatial dimension and an explicit method in the temporal dimension. This algorithm was tested using synthetic quasilinear models and a variational model of the 2D electromagnetic dynamics in the presence of magnetic fields. Notably, the algorithm exhibited excellent performance and stability, while demonstrating second-order accuracy in both temporal and spatial dimensions.

A class of difference schemes, including the SDIMSIM method, has been previously studied. Building upon existing research, a new variable stepsize variant of SDIMSIMs for standard ordinary differential equations is presented and analyzed.

In a Banach space, the existence and uniqueness of a Hermitian solution to the Lyapunov equation are proven, along with its application in proving the existence, uniqueness, and stability of solutions to the differential equation, given the generator's resolvent and invertibility of the solution to the Lyapunov equation.

To investigate muon-like particles as potential antigravity candidates that interact with matter, a new calculator called MuMuPy has been created. This tool enables researchers to calculate the differential and total cross-sections for muon-antimuon pair scattering off nuclei and atoms, and their interaction with molecules, using an approximation method. The calculator's utility is highlighted by a case study involving dimuonium, where it's used to determine its interaction characteristics with gaseous helium.

Portfolio managers assess investment success through two main criteria: 
the overall level of wealth created and the level of wealth relative to a benchmark. Traditional performance evaluation methods, such as maximizing utility of a portfolio's value, focus on absolute performance, while tracking benchmark beta measures relative returns. However, these methods are mutually exclusive. In contrast, mean-CVaR optimization only considers one of these aspects. This paper proposes a novel performance evaluation approach, utility of the p-th power of absolute or relative assets. By incorporating this approach, investors can choose between maximizing a portfolio's performance in absolute terms, matching benchmark performance in relative terms, or a combination of both. We derive an analytical solution for this portfolio's optimal allocation and investigate its properties, providing insights into how it behaves under different scenarios.

Galaxies are widely recognized as the primary reservoirs of baryons in the universe. However, it is hypothesized that many small galaxies may have expelled a significant portion of their gas during past supernovae events. Consequently, they may be surrounded by hot, diffuse ionized gas (DIG) or stripped of it entirely due to ram pressure. To investigate this, a research study examines the intergalactic medium of 12 dwarf galaxies using data from X-ray and radio observations. The study reveals that approximately 70% of these galaxies host kiloparsec-scale hot gas halos, which could be replenished by the gas's accretion from the intergalactic medium. The hot gas is observed to be misaligned with the galaxy's angular momentum, suggesting it is not the result of galactic outflows. Furthermore, one galaxy, M32, is suspected to have previously experienced a gas expulsion event, as indicated by its radio emission of synchrotron origin. The study also explores the potential application of a novel method to detect the hot gas around galaxies with lower X-ray sensitivity, such as M32.

We examine the resilience of fermionic quasiparticles when interacting with local bosons, utilizing a model where a non-interacting fermion gas is linked to a single vibrational mode. Our research reveals that even a minimal coupling between fermions and phonons can result in an abrupt disappearance of quasiparticles without a phonon gap opening or a quasiparticle renormalization mass surge. This phenomenon is associated with an unanticipated fermionic quasiparticle collapse, where it is no longer possible to describe an excitation as a single fermion dressed by phonons. Unlike the traditional Kondo model, the collapse does not involve the formation of a local moment, nor does it occur at a finite temperature. These findings are verified through the self-consistent self-energy approximation and the diagrammatic self-energy approximation, which also shows that the spectral function exhibits a distinct minimum without a divergent behavior.

The divergence function, which measures how quickly the distance from the identity grows in terms of word length, provides an effective tool for distinguishing among finitely generated groups. Our study focuses on the divergence of all generalised Thompson groups over infinite sets and their full and half-transform groups, in relation to braided Thompson groups, which yield the fastest possible divergence in this context.

This article presents the comprehensive implementation and customization process of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture, specifically tailored for a German question-answer task. To achieve this, the code utilizes key libraries, including PyTorch, transformers, sentence-transformers, and faiss. Furthermore, the article showcases a more efficient approach to configuring the RAG architecture, incorporating gradient-checkpointing and mixed-precision training techniques, while also reducing memory usage, and outlines the adoption of the efficient-attn architecture from the DPR paper.

This study derives a simple and direct proof of Askey's theorem on the asymptotic behavior of polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to a weight distribution that includes a logarithmic influence. Additionally, this investigation develops new inequalities for these polynomials and proves sharp Markov and Bernstein inequalities, as well as the Markov conjecture proposed by Krein.

A multitude of studies rely on crowdsourcing, yet the quality of crowd workers varies greatly, and the impact of this variability on research outcomes remains uncertain. To address this, the objective is to develop a reliable method for identifying top-tier workers. The evaluation was conducted on 12 qualified and unqualified workers using 12 tasks from Qualtrics on MTurk. The results revealed that existing reputation systems, such as MTurk's, fail to identify top performers. Conversely, the 'eBay-style' bidding system demonstrated the most success in identifying qualified workers. Furthermore, the data suggests that individual differences among workers are significant, while group disparities appear to be less pronounced.

Video retrieval systems that analyze both audio and visual data are crucial for a range of applications, but existing methods often struggle with processing long texts and long videos. To address this limitation, a new model called TS-Net has been developed, which uses an efficient transformer-based approach to process input media of varying lengths. TS-Net's effectiveness relies on its ability to reorganize the order of features through shifting and selecting mechanisms, which significantly reduces the computational complexity of the transformer. To further enhance the performance of TS-Net, a new model called TS2-Net has been created by incorporating clip selection and motion perception capabilities. By combining these features, TS2-Net achieves state-of-the results on multiple video retrieval benchmarks, regardless of the length of the text and video.

Within a supersymmetric $R$-parity-violating minimal flavor-violation framework, a new class of $\Delta C = 2$ operators are introduced through an $\tilde{t}_1$-$\tilde{\tau}_1$ snuark, which mediates the $D$-meson decays $D$-$\tilde{t}_1$ and the $\tilde{t}_1$-mediated $D$-$\tau^+ \tau^-$ decay. The considerations are based on the $\tilde{t}_1$ mass of 100 GeV and a tan beta of 10. The decays $D \to \tilde{t}_1$-mediated $D \to \tau^+ \tau^-$ and $D \to \tilde{t}_1$ are found to be the most significant, which can be detected at the High-Luminosity LHC and future $t$ factories.

A Hybrid Random Graph is formed by combining the Preferential Attachment and Uniform Attachment models. Initially, a single node is established, and a sequence of additional nodes is added one at a time. At each stage, an existing node is randomly selected based on a mixture of preferential and uniform attachments. The resulting directed graph is analyzed, with an emphasis on the behavior of long paths, including maximum degrees of nodes, of the directed graph. The initial set of nodes for study includes a single vertex with in-degree one, resulting in a distinct graph structure. The analysis reveals that, in a Homophily Hybrid Random Graph, the maximum degree of nodes asymptotically behaves like a Gumbel-distributed random variable under the given attachment process. The initial setup of this model, with a single vertex having in-degree one, is essential for defining the model and analyzing its properties. The results of the study are derived from a new analytical method, leveraging the initial graph structure of nodes with out-degree one, arranged in a tree. The method enables identifying the initial node that generated a specific node, allowing the analysis of the initial graph structure of nodes with out-degree one, including its relation to a corresponding directed tree. The study also includes additional results on path lengths, including an analysis of the initial setup of nodes for study, with an emphasis on nodes that have out-degree one, resulting in a directed tree.
